items.title: Battle turns
items.summary: The half-second timing units used to register and resolve battle actions.

content.heading: The smallest timing unit
body: The simulator measures battle timing in turns. One turn lasts 0.5 seconds, and Fast Attack durations are expressed as whole turns.
An action can be selected only when its Pokémon is ready. A Fast Attack keeps that Pokémon occupied for its full duration before another action can be registered.

content.heading: Read the timeline
body: Each numbered cell is one turn. The same six turns equal three seconds of battle time.

content.heading: Key point
body: Turn numbers describe ordering. Seconds describe elapsed time. Keep the two separate when reconstructing an incident.

items.title: Fast Attack duration
items.summary: How a Fast Attack's duration controls action availability and alignment.

content.heading: Duration locks the user
body: A Fast Attack starts on its registration turn and occupies the user for the attack's listed duration. A 2-turn attack and a 3-turn attack therefore reach their next action windows at different times.

content.heading: Two-turn versus three-turn alignment
body: The rows begin together. They realign after six turns, when three 2-turn moves and two 3-turn moves have completed.

content.heading: Why it matters
body: Duration determines both the next legal action window and where Fast Attack impact appears on the reconstructed timeline.

items.title: Fast Attack impact
items.summary: When Fast Attack damage and energy register in the simulator timeline.

content.heading: Impact turn
body: The impact turn is calculated as start turn + duration − 1. At that impact, the attack's damage and energy gain are resolved together.
Fast Attack events that impact on the same turn are evaluated from the state at the start of that impact phase, so simultaneous damage can produce a simultaneous knockout.

content.heading: Three-turn Fast Attack
body: A move registered on turn 1 with duration 3 reaches its impact on turn 3.

content.heading: Key point
body: Registration, impact, and the next ready turn are separate facts. Use the event marker and state snapshot together when reviewing timing.

items.title: Energy generation and spending
items.summary: How Fast Attack energy is gained, capped, and spent on Charged Attacks.

content.heading: Gain at Fast Attack impact
body: Fast Attack energy is added when that Fast Attack reaches its impact. Stored energy is capped at 100; any gain beyond the cap is not retained.
A Charged Attack becomes available only when the Pokémon is ready to act and has at least the attack's energy cost. Resolving that action spends the listed cost.

Energy gained by a Pokémon remains with that Pokémon until it is spent on a Charged Attack or the Pokémon faints. Energy cannot be transferred to another Pokémon, and switching the Pokémon out does not cause it to lose energy.

content.heading: Example
body: A Pokémon at 96 energy uses a Fast Attack that grants 8 energy. The resulting total is 100, not 104. A 45-energy Charged Attack would then leave 55 energy.

content.heading: Key point
body: Having enough energy is necessary but not sufficient: the Pokémon must also be at a legal action window.

items.title: Charged Attack Priority (CAP)
items.summary: How simultaneous Charged Attack registrations are ordered by current Attack.

content.heading: Compare current Attack
body: When both sides register a Charged Attack in the same decision window, the simulator orders the Pokémon with the higher current Attack first. The comparison uses battle Attack after active stat-stage modifiers.
A displayed CP value does not decide CAP. The relevant value is the Pokémon's calculated Attack in the reconstructed state.

content.heading: Resolution order
body: Both Charged Attacks are registered in the same window.
Current Attack is compared and the higher-Attack side resolves first.
The battle state is checked before the second registered action continues.

content.heading: Equal Attack
body: Equal calculated Attack is retained as a tied-CAP condition in review metadata. Treat the tie itself as relevant evidence rather than inferring an advantage from species name or CP.

items.title: Attack and Defense stages
items.summary: The bounded battle modifiers applied to Attack and Defense.

content.heading: Stage range
body: Attack and Defense stages are tracked independently from −4 through +4. Effects cannot raise or lower a stat beyond those limits.
Positive Attack stages increase outgoing damage calculations. Positive Defense stages increase the defending value; negative stages act in the opposite direction.

content.heading: Multiplier pattern
body: The simulator uses (4 + stage) / 4 for non-negative stages and 4 / (4 − stage) for negative stages. For example, +1 is 1.25× and −1 is 0.8×.

content.heading: CAP interaction
body: Because CAP compares current Attack, an Attack buff or debuff can change which side resolves a simultaneous Charged Attack first.
